transcript:
Header:
Date: 2025-06-30
Start time: 15:00 PDT
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Priya Shah (Redwood AE), Evan Liu (Redwood SE), Marta Ruiz (Redwood DevRel); Marcus Reed (Huxley Labs - Lead ML), Sara Kim (Huxley - Platform), Tom Alvarez (Huxley - CTO), Leah Ortiz (Huxley - DevOps)
Recording id: ff-20250630-9bdf

Summary:
Quick sandbox onboarding + SDK walkthrough (Python + TypeScript), auth patterns for sandbox -> VPC/private, KMS/HSM options, and a lightweight perf spike plan. We demoed the SDK quickstart, env var approaches, CI secret rotation, and discussed Optimize suggestions for batching/quantization. Action items and perf run scheduling at the end.

Topics covered:
- SDK quickstart (py/ts) and sample repo layout
- Auth in sandbox (api key) vs. private (VPC + mTLS + KMS)
- CI/CD secrets, GCP Workload Identity and Azure MSI notes
- Console routes: model pinning & rollout, cost/latency dashboards
- Redwood Optimize suggestions: batching, prefix caching, quant profiles
- Security: SOC2, SAML SSO, audit logs, egress controls, HSM integrations

Transcript Body:
[00:00] Priya Shah: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I think we have about 50 minutes, um, we'll run through a fast sandbox demo of the SDKs and then leave time for security questions and the perf run plan. Sound good?
[00:18] Marcus Reed: Yep that works, thanks Priya. We're mostly interested in how fast we can get an internal sandbox up and then move to our VPC private deployment.
[00:29] Evan Liu: Cool. I'll start with the Python quickstart in the sandbox environment, and then switch to TypeScript for the CI example. Quick note — I'll be using the sample repo we shared, it's in the drive Marta mentioned.
[00:42] Sara Kim: One ask up front — our infra needs an Azure key vault + HSM integration eventually, so, any blockers there?
[00:49] Marta Ruiz: Totally, we'll show the KMS options. Redwood supports customer-managed keys via KMS/HSM integrations and we can point to our HSM partner flows; sometimes the terminology in the docs gets a little different so we'll clarify.
[01:05] Evan Liu: Ok pulling up the Python notebook. First step is pip install redwood-sdk (note: package name in sandbox is redwood-infer-dev, but we have both py and ts packages). Then we set REDWOOD_API_KEY as an env var. For sandbox quickstarts that's typical — api key in env.
[01:28] Leah Ortiz: For CI, we want to avoid storing keys in repo. We use GitHub actions and prefer Workload Identity federation for GCP.
[01:35] Evan Liu: Yes, for GCP Workload Identity we show a sample runner step: fetch secret from Secret Manager bound to the workload identity, then export as REDWOOD_API_KEY in the job. For Azure you can use Managed Service Identity (MSI) to fetch secrets from Key Vault.
[01:54] Tom Alvarez: Is there a short-lived token option rather than long-lived API keys?
[02:00] Priya Shah: We do support ephemeral tokens for certain private deployments; we can present the session broker flow. That's more common for Dedicated/Private. For hosted sandbox the typical flow is api key with rotation.
[02:14] Marcus Reed: Ok, show us the code.
[02:18] Evan Liu: Sure. In Python: from redwood import RedwoodClient; client = RedwoodClient(api_key=os.environ['REDWOOD_API_KEY']); resp = client.generate("Summarize: " + doc_text, model="rwd-2-small"); print(resp.text) — note the model name in the sandbox may be prefixed with sandbox-. The SDK handles streaming too, via client.stream(...).
[02:45] Sara Kim: You said rwd-2-small — that's Redwood's internal shorthand, right? We call it differently in our tracker.
[02:51] Marta Ruiz: Yeah the names can get munged between docs and the console — apologies, the console shows the full catalog name. We'll include a mapping file in the shared drive so you can map model aliases.
[03:05] Evan Liu: Switching to the TypeScript snippet now. It's similar: import { RedwoodClient } from '@redwood/infer'; const client = new RedwoodClient({ apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY }); await client.generate({ model: 'rwd-2-small', input: '...' })
[03:28] Marcus Reed: What about prefix caching — we have a lot of repeated system prompts in our calls.
[03:33] Evan Liu: Good question. Redwood has automatic prefix/KV cache for repeated prefixes. For high-repeat patterns you can enable more aggressive caching via console config per-route. That reduces tokens and latency. One caveat: caching is per-model variant and sequence length bucket, so if you frequently change prompt length you see cache misses.
[03:58] Leah Ortiz: Any gotchas moving from sandbox to our VPC private? Network egress?
[04:03] Priya Shah: For Private we provide a private control plane and you can route inference traffic over peered VPCs. There's optional egress controls and dedicated capacity. The onboarding we do for Private includes a network runbook.
[04:16] Tom Alvarez: On the security checklist, we need SOC2 Type II, SAML SSO, RBAC, and audit log retention to 1 year.
[04:26] Marta Ruiz: Redwood is SOC2-certified, SAML and SCIM are supported for SSO and provisioning. Audit logs are available and we can increase retention as part of an enterprise package. We'll share the compliance matrix.
[04:41] Marcus Reed: Can you show the console: model routes, pinning, and rollouts? We want to do canary tests.
[04:48] Evan Liu: Yep. (Shares screen) Here's the console route editor — you can pin a model version, set canary percentage, and a fallback policy that routes traffic to a cheaper quantized variant if latency spikes or capacity is constrained. Invocation traces and per-token cost appear on the route dashboard.
[05:12] Sara Kim: That fallback thing — does it preserve responses or do we get degraded quality?
[05:17] Evan Liu: There's a tradeoff. Quantized variants may slightly degrade output in specific evals; Redwood Optimize will recommend which workloads are safe to quantize based on your eval set. We also have automatic regression alerts if quality slips beyond your threshold.
[05:38] Marcus Reed: Cool. For the perf run, we want throughput numbers for short (64 token) and long (1024 token) sequences on Dedicated.
[05:45] Priya Shah: We'll set up a perf run — typical plan is small sample data, one dedicated pool config and a fallback policy. We'll provide a spreadsheet of expected token cost and latency per model.
[06:00] Evan Liu: Back to SDK details — for local dev we include a docker-compose that runs a lightweight reverse proxy that injects the REDWOOD_API_KEY for you; it's handy for quick pairing. But in CI you should use secret fetchers instead of checked-in env files.
[06:20] Leah Ortiz: Show the docker-compose?
[06:23] Evan Liu: Sure, quick share. (describes) Service: dev-proxy, image: redwood/dev-proxy:latest, env_file: .env.local (ignored by git). It proxies/rewrites requests so dev can use localhost:8080. It's just a helper — not for prod.
[06:45] Tom Alvarez: How do we handle KMS on private? We require that all model inputs are not stored unencrypted and that keys are under our control.
[06:54] Marta Ruiz: For Private deployments we support customer-managed keys. We can integrate with AWS KMS, Azure Key Vault, or an HSM provider. You can configure envelope encryption; Redwood can avoid persisting plaintext logs if required. We'll include Huxley-specific notes in the security doc we send.
[07:15] Marcus Reed: Any implications for latency if encryption is enforced at rest and in transit?
[07:20] Evan Liu: Encryption at rest is mostly irrelevant for inference latency. For in-transit mutual TLS or additional brokered short-lived tokens there's a very small auth handshake cost but nothing at token-gen time. The bigger latency factors are model size, batching, and kernel selection.
[07:39] Sara Kim: Speaking of batching, how do we tune for low-latency at low QPS versus high throughput?
[07:45] Evan Liu: Redwood has autoscaling with a smart batching runtime. For latency-sensitive routes you can set a max batching window (like 5-10 ms) to keep per-request latency tight; for throughput you can increase the window to 50-100 ms. Optimize will recommend settings based on your observed sequence lengths.
[08:05] Marcus Reed: Let's talk about the sample perf run. We want an initial smoke test in sandbox, then a dedicated run with 2x GPUs. What's realistic to get initial numbers?
[08:13] Priya Shah: We can run a 2-hour dedicated perf with your sample dataset. We'll include both short/long runs and a mixed workload. After that, we'll share a cost/latency breakdown at token granularity.
[08:28] Tom Alvarez: Great. On billing, do we see per-route cost? We want chargeback.
[08:33] Marta Ruiz: Yes, the console has per-route and per-token cost breakdown. You can also export usage by token and user id for internal billing.
[08:45] Leah Ortiz: On SSO provisioning, we use SCIM to sync groups. How do you map RBAC to our groups?
[08:52] Evan Liu: Redwood supports SCIM group sync. You can map SCIM groups to roles in the console (viewer, developer, admin). We'll share the SCIM schema and a sample mapping.
[09:06] Marcus Reed: Any limits on model uploads or custom fine-tunes in Private?
[09:11] Priya Shah: For Private you can host private models. There are storage considerations for large fine-tunes; we size the pool accordingly. FTs are supported but we recommend version pinning and ephemeral KV caches for inference.
[09:26] Evan Liu: One more demo piece: I'll show a simple TypeScript streaming example that attaches to a websocket and updates UI on token events. (demonstrates) The SDK exposes client.streamEvents(callback) and you'll receive partialToken events.
[09:50] Sara Kim: Nice. Is the streaming protocol standard wss?
[09:53] Evan Liu: It's wss with an auth header. Locally you can tunnel, in prod we recommend using the SDK which abstracts that for you.
[10:03] Marcus Reed: Ok we have a few security follow-ups: data retention policy, option to disable logs, SOC2 report, and a technical contact for HSM integration.
[10:11] Priya Shah: We'll send the SOC2 report and a security contact. Regarding retention, we can configure retention windows and a no-logging option for specific routes. We'll note all four items in the next steps.
[10:25] Tom Alvarez: Is there a way to test regressions automatically when we change prompts or models?
[10:31] Marta Ruiz: Yes, Redwood Optimize supports eval sets and continuous quality monitoring; you can tie alerts to a prompt set so that if a model change reduces a metric we trigger a rollback or alert.
[10:44] Sara Kim: For the perf run spreadsheet, can you include expected token accounting with batching effects modeled?
[10:50] Evan Liu: We'll include token accounting and an expected cost estimate that factors in batching savings. It won't be perfect but it's a solid starting point.
[10:58] Marcus Reed: Anything we should avoid in the sandbox when preparing for Private?
[11:02] Priya Shah: Avoid baking long-lived keys into images and avoid experimenting with large fine-tunes in the public sandbox if the data is sensitive. Use synthetic or redacted data. We'll provide a migration checklist in the doc.
[11:18] Leah Ortiz: Quick question on CIDR ranges — for peering we need to confirm the IPs you'll use for the private pool.
[11:23] Evan Liu: We'll provide the private pool CIDR and run a network checklist with your infra team. That's part of the Private onboarding.
[11:31] Tom Alvarez: For the initial sandbox, how fast can we be live?
[11:34] Priya Shah: We can spin up a sandbox and keys in under an hour; with your team following the quickstart you could be hitting the API the same day. Private onboarding is multi-week depending on approvals.
[11:46] Marcus Reed: Ok great. Let's circle back to the SDK repo structure and sample files.
[11:51] Evan Liu: Repo layout we recommend: /examples/python/quickstart.py, /examples/ts/quickstart.ts, /docker/dev-proxy/, /ci/workflows/*, /docs/secrets.md. We'll put a template .env.example with REDWOOD_API_KEY and optional REDWOOD_ENDPOINT for private routes.
[12:16] Sara Kim: Any naming conventions for route names to make the console dashboards cleaner?
[12:20] Marta Ruiz: Use /service-name/route/purpose, e.g., /search/answer/primary. It helps with per-route cost mapping and alerting.
[12:31] Evan Liu: Small demo of the Optimize tab — it gave us a suggestion to lower batch window for route /search/answer/primary and to enable a quant profile for the recommendation workload. It also surfaced a regression for a prompt in last week's run.
[12:50] Marcus Reed: When you say quant profile, do you have specific quant formats supported?
[12:54] Evan Liu: We support int8 and mixed quant profiles; the console shows expected delta vs baseline and recommends safety checks. We'll include the quant recommendation sheet in the shared folder.
[13:09] Leah Ortiz: Are there SDK helpers for token counting and truncation?
[13:13] Evan Liu: Yes, both py/ts SDKs include a tokenizer util; we also ship a prepackaged truncation helper that returns safe prefixes to keep under limits.
[13:26] Tom Alvarez: For auditing, we need request-level logs that include anonymized user id and route only, not full prompts. Is that possible?
[13:35] Marta Ruiz: Yes you can configure logging redaction rules per route; there's also an option to hash or redact prompt text while retaining metadata. We'll add an example config.
[13:50] Marcus Reed: Anything else on the SDK? Library compatibility with our node LTS?
[13:55] Evan Liu: The TypeScript package supports Node 16+; Python supports 3.8+. We test against LTS versions.
[14:05] Sara Kim: For local testing of streaming, is there any recommended frontend sample?
[14:09] Evan Liu: We have a small React sample under /examples/ts/react-stream that uses the streaming client to append tokens as they arrive. We'll share the snippet.
[14:21] Marcus Reed: OK that's helpful. Let's talk timeline: we want a smoke sandbox this week and a dedicated perf next week.
[14:28] Priya Shah: We'll target sandbox today — our action item is to send the sandbox config and sample scripts within 48 hours. For the dedicated perf we can schedule the week of 2025-07-07.
[14:40] Tom Alvarez: Security contact?
[14:42] Marta Ruiz: Marta Ruiz is listed as the Redwood security/DevRel contact for questions; we'll also include an enterprise security engineer on the thread.
[14:51] Marcus Reed: One last question: any vendor lock-in concerns with console route names or SDK calls we should be aware of?
[14:57] Evan Liu: SDK calls are standard generate/stream patterns; the main lock-in surface is model pin names and route configs. We recommend abstracting calls in a small internal client library so you can swap endpoints if needed.
[15:12] Priya Shah: Ok, to recap next steps — Redwood will: 1) share sandbox config, docker-compose, and example py/ts scripts; 2) send SOC2 and compliance matrix; 3) provide perf-run spreadsheet and schedule; Huxley will: a) share KMS preference and data residency constraints, b) confirm perf run dataset.
[15:35] Marcus Reed: Sounds good. Thanks all.
[15:40] Priya Shah: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up with the links.

End of recording.
